title: Pompeii: 20,000 People Died in a Single Morning
api_title: Pompeii: 20,000 People Died in a Single Morning
api_description:
In a single morning, 20,000 people died where they stood — no war, no plague. The mountain did it. This is Pompeii, the city time forgot to destroy, walked street by street.

I am Professor Adrian, and what amazes me about Pompeii is not the destruction. It is how ordinary it all was: bread in the ovens, election posters on the walls, a dog chained at its post. Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote it down letter by letter — we still read his account today. In 1863 Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the ash and gave the dead back their faces. And in 2018, a single charcoal inscription quietly moved the date of the disaster itself.

Pompeii is not just a tragedy about a volcano. It is a mirror — and a warning, because Vesuvius is still breathing above three million people.

title: The Payphone at Mile 61
api_title: The Payphone at Mile 61
api_description:
A dead payphone rang at 3:33 in the morning — and the caller ID showed my mother's phone number. She had been dead for eleven years.

I'm Jack Doyle. For three years I worked the night shift at Mile 61, a gas station off Interstate 40 with forty miles of nothing on either side. Bolted to the brick wall by the restrooms sat a gray payphone that had been dead since 1994. Everybody in the county knew it was dead. Then, on October the fourteenth, it rang.

Honestly, this one genuinely scared me, because it happened to me. The voice on that line warned me about a leaking gas pump, a card skimmer, a woman being followed — and it was right every single time. But on the fourteenth night, it told me who it was. And what happens when it finally counts down to one.

The police investigated. A private investigator dug deeper. The previous owners admitted they'd received a letter too — and never told anyone. In 2019 the Broadduses sold at a nearly $400,000 loss. Reportedly, the new owners got a letter as well.

I still think about this one every time I pass a for sale sign. If you love real unsolved horror, you're in the right place.
